358.t: The Story & Clark player piano and playing for classmates
358.s: Growing up in the Depression with a player piano near the Nat Cole family's neighborhood, he imitated Ellington and played at school for admiring girls.
358.q: Well we had a piano in the house when I was young. We were, and actually I was born, I was lucky because I was born in the depression time. My father had his own business then, and we had a piano, and we had a Victrola. But the piano — as a matter of fact we lived in the neighborhood where the Nat…

358.t: Starting on piano at 13: player piano and Ellington records
358.s: Simmons began around age 13 by ear on the family player piano, picking out Duke Ellington pieces and working into after-hours tunes.
358.q: When I knew that I was what I wanted to do, well that was like two questions you just asked me, because I guess I started doing it before I knew that was what I wanted to do. So I started doing it I guess around 13 years old. So I was kind of an old starter. I started by ear. You know we just…

615.s: His parents loved music without being musicians; their records of Goodman, Basie, Miller and Dorsey drew him in.
615.q: I’d say they were musical but they weren’t musicians. You know they had a lot of good records around the house. They had everything from jazz to light classical stuff and some show tunes and stuff like that. And when I was very young I came across some old 45 rpm records and one of them I remember…

803.t: Father's 78s and the school music camp aha moment
803.s: Cunningham says his father's love of early jazz was their connection, and that playing Louis Armstrong tunes at a school music camp at 16-17 showed him people respond to the music.
803.q: Yes. Absolutely. Well let’s get deep really quickly then. So my dad, he was a big jazz fan. He loved all jazz but he especially loved the early style. Louis Armstrong, Fats Waller, Mills Brothers. And he had a great 78 collection. He didn’t have a huge one, it was maybe 50 or 60, 78s but you know…

1016.t: Childhood: parents' music, the shiny alto and starting on clarinet
1016.s: His parents danced to big band records and TV bands, he wanted the shiny alto sax in a shop window but started on clarinet, and Maynard liked all music.
1016.q: I don’t know. I think it was, when I think back the earliest thing I can remember was that it was something that was fun. You know what I mean? Like sports were fun. Other things — the music was fun, I had friends that were fun, but I do remember being — my parents, my mother was a cook like for a…

981.t: Records at home and the decision to become a musician
981.s: Music filled his family's homes, from Charlie Parker 78s to Garner, Vaughan and Roach, and his father let him be. In his senior year he vowed to become a musician. His uncle then called him for a gig at 17.
981.q: My mother played piano. Her father played piano. But my father played, and my aunts played, we call it the Victrola, the record player. So I had — my father made sure I heard every kind of music that ever existed.

599.t: Growing up on guitar, Brubeck, Monk and big bands at home
599.s: Gates calls jazz life an adventure, turned pro at 39, and recalls his father's records and early Brubeck and Monk albums.
599.q: An adventure. And interesting. But I wouldn’t have it any other way. I did a lot of other things before I did this. I started to do this on a professional level at 39 years old, which is about three or four years ago.

616.t: Childhood music: singing, Lawrence Welk and choosing the bass
616.s: Gilmore recalls singing harmony with his parents, hearing the Metropolitan Opera, and deciding on the bass after a slap-bass solo on Lawrence Welk.
616.q: Well I mean I can tell you from my very early origins that I remember I was involved with music somewhat. I remember when I was a kid, me having a pretty good voice and singing harmony parts with my mother and father as we used to take trips and drive together. And they would sing like the old…

513.t: Moving toward jazz and his mother's influence
513.s: Around 1953-54 he listened to R&B and classical; his mother pushed him, and the coolest high school kids liked jazz.
513.q: It was about 1953 or ‘54 when I was either thirteen or fourteen years old. The funny thing is that I had been listening to rhythm & blues before that. And I was hanging out with the kids my age of course and that’s what they listened to and that’s what I listened to, and I also listened to…

212.t: The 'Madame Butterfly' record from his first-grade teacher
212.s: Story of a record from teacher Mrs. Ferrell, his misjudgment of it, and his discovery of opera on Saturday radio.
212.q: Oh. Well being the teacher’s pet that I was in the first grade, I was helping my teacher clean out her closet and I found some recordings. It was about 1947, ’46. And as far as I knew, records were the blues and Louis Jordan and all that sort of thing. And I knew that white people didn’t listen to…

543.t: First hearing jazz on a clip-on radio as a child
543.s: His father gave him a clip-on radio at about eight and he heard jazz, probably Mack the Knife, on San Francisco radio.
543.q: You know I sort of do and sort of don’t. I remember my father gave me one of those clip- on unpowered radios. I don’t know if you remember that. It just has an alligator clip, you put it on your lampshade next to your bed and it receives stations. So I must have been like eight years old or…

657.s: His mother took him to shows and bought Lester Young and Coltrane records.
657.q: Yeah, and as far as practicing and all that, and I mean we went to shows and I went to see Ray Charles and a lot of the shows that came to Utica she bought me records, like Lester Young records and John Coltrane records, which I didn’t check out at first. You know I’d put it on and I’d be like well…

341.t: Country and Irish music at home; finding jazz on the radio
341.s: Her mother played country and Irish music; she stumbled on jazz radio, hearing Booker Ervin, and says nobody really chooses jazz as a career.
341.ch: Growing up in Endicott and learning drums
341.q: She likes Irish folk music too. Her family, there are a lot of Irish relatives. I like that also. But every single morning we woke up and one of those two styles of music was blaring through the house. I just remember also being a kid and spinning the dial on my radio in bed one night, I couldn’t…

442.t: Seeing the Alan Freed rock and roll show at the Paramount
442.s: At 14 Morell sees a rock and roll revue on Broadway and fixates on the backing drummer.
442.q: Not really. I just knew that I wanted to be a musician, at a very early age, 14 years old. I went to a big show at the Paramount Theater on Broadway. And I was just in awe. I saw the drummer up there playing. It was Alan Freed, I don’t know if you have any rock & roll fans.

100.t: Leaving Austria and first Fats Waller concert in Copenhagen
100.s: After the Anschluss he reached Denmark and in 1938 his mother took him to a Fats Waller concert, his first live jazz.
100.q: I was eight when Hitler took over Austria. I was nine, and fairly recent in Copenhagen when my mother, bless her, decided that I might enjoy a Fats Waller concert. Fats was touring Scandinavia, and she got tickets for Fats Waller in 1938, in the fall of 1938, and that was my first, you know, real,…

963.t: No single aha moment: early listening and the drum corps
963.s: He had no defining moment; he recalls his mother's Al Hirt records, his sister's Bill Evans and Miles, and the drum corps and bugle that kept him off the streets.
963.q: I think it would be nice to say yes and like many artists can say, “When I was in fourth grade somebody came through town and I was knocked out and never forgot it.” I don’t think I ever had one of those. And I’m a little maybe different from a lot of other great — not great but other artists, that…

557.t: Starting on drums, the Army, and drummer influences
557.s: Roker began on marching drums at six, took up a drum set after being drafted in 1952, and names Kenny Clarke, Papa Jo Jones, Philly Joe Jones and Specs Wright as influences.
557.q: Well I started playing drums when I was about maybe six years old. And mostly military drums, marching band, stuff like that. And then I got drafted into the Army and that’s when I decided I wanted to play swing — a set of drums. So everybody that played drums was a big influence on me you know…

586.t: Oldies radio, classical guitar and her brother's tapes
586.s: Born 1976, she listened to oldies and Segovia, studied classical guitar from age eight, and was given unmarked jazz tapes by her brother.
586.q: Well I listened a lot to the oldies, ‘50s and ‘60s type of music. There is a radio station around my area, it’s called Big D 103, and so I would always listen to that all the time. My brother listened to a lot of the current music but I never really did. I mostly enjoyed the oldies. And I think,…

600.t: How music grabbed him: playing by ear, his mother's records, starting jazz at 15
600.s: Rydin has played piano all his life, learned by ear, heard Basie, Armstrong and Ellington via his mother, and began playing jazz at 15-16.
600.q: First of all I’ve been playing piano all my life. So I have memories as a little child playing by ear the children’s songs. And play by ear, that’s what I still do. So my mother listened to jazz, to Basie, Louis Armstrong, Ellington, those kind of things. So I got it by the record. I wouldn’t say I…

548.t: Growing up with his brother, 78s and hearing the masters
548.s: His older brother's drums and trumpet, parents' 78s, Armstrong and Bix LPs, hearing Ellington, Armstrong, Miles and Coltrane live in Chicago; supportive university parents.
548.q: Well yeah, I mean not them specifically. Basically how I got into listening to jazz was I guess through my older brother. I mean our parents had some 78s that belonged to I guess their parents. And it was a very mixed bag. But in it were some kind of interesting things. Nothing great, but I mean…

549.t: Why jazz attracted him at age four or five
549.s: He explains the music's pull and his access through Hollis, Queens, comparing it with childhood enthusiasm for sports.
549.ch: Basie alumni and childhood in Hollis
549.q: Well why the music attracted me is probably something inside me that is not explainable. Why I had access to the music is probably a combination of my parents — let’s not forget Marjorie Schaap — and the proximity of the musicians who were making jazz to the Hollis Queens neighborhood where we…

976.t: Adoring Chet Baker; brother Klaus; wanting to be a dancer
976.s: Chet Baker's singing brought her to music; her brother Klaus drummed in his European rhythm section and quit over his drug use; she once wanted to dance.
976.q: Oh, I adore him. Because he sang like he played. I totally adored him. My father was a professor so whenever we came home early from school, my brother Klaus and me — Klaus played drums in my room and I sang. And we had a Chet Baker record going. And I just loved the softness of his voice. He loved…

716.t: Earliest music memory: the Ink Spots and Jimmy Blythe's lick
716.s: At age four he heard the Ink Spots and later recognized their opener in a Ma Rainey record with Jimmy Blythe; Rowe calls it a community lick.
716.q: I can’t remember not liking music at all or not responding to it. I guess sort of an answer to your question is what are my earliest music memories and there’s one that really sticks out. I was born in 1937 so I would have been four I think when I heard the Ink Spots I guess it was, singing “I…

702.t: Big band music at home, first trombone, and seeing Ellington's band
702.s: Turré says jazz had his heart early; his parents met at a Count Basie dance, he watched Dizzy, Bird and Armstrong on TV, started trombone in fourth grade, and was taken to see the real Ellington band.
702.ch: Bay Area youth and early listening
702.q: Not as a career, no. But I enjoyed it and I played it too, but you know jazz had my heart from an early age, early age. You know my mom and dad met at a Count Basie dance. And we had big band music, that was the dance music of their day you know. So you know we had big band music in the house all…

447.t: Musical family and the decision to be a musician
447.s: Vaché's father and brother were musicians and he never considered anything else; born 1953, he grew up on records.
447.q: Oh gosh. Well I come from a musical family. My brother is a professional musician, my father was at one point a professional musician but felt he couldn’t support a family on it so ended up just working weekends and stuff and playing. He played at Nick’s and Condon’s back in the ‘30s and so forth.…

552.t: Childhood music at home and the Hampton Jazz Festival
552.s: Wilson was inspired by his father's records and by festivals in Hampton; his father sang in a choir but did not play.
552.q: That’s a good question. You know I think it was just being inspired very young, being exposed to the music by my father, who is a music enthusiast and had all kinds of music around the house. The first record I remember hearing live was Ahmad Jamal “Live at the Pershing” and of course with…

108.t: Dreaming of orchestral playing and the Tchaikovsky moment
108.s: He wanted to be a symphonic player; his father's radio listening and playing Tchaikovsky's Pathetique in the band moves him.
108.ch: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
108.q: Yeah, you were asking me about that. It’s funny. I had heard – I used to love to listen to orchestras. My father listened to all kinds of music from the time I was a little kid. He used to listen. On the radio, you had all these bands. We had an old Zenith radio. My father would switch from one…

378.t: Boyhood friends and Edison records of George Hamilton Green
378.s: No radio; the family had thick Edison records of Ray Miller's orchestra and xylophonist George Hamilton Green, and he met other musicians such as Frank Skinner and Mel Hewlett as he got older.
378.q: As I got a little older I met some. Course there was Mel Healt who was in that town and the Skinner boys, you know Frank Skinner. They -- he had the Ranger, he had three brothers that worked in Macedosia, which is right down the River a little ways --

381.t: Father's record collection and the first record he played
381.s: His father collected records; he remembers the Victrola accident and his first record, Running Wild by the Ferde Grofe orchestra.
381.q: Well, I was climbing up one day to play a record -- I don't remember what record it was -- and I slipped and burst my lip. And my father went out and bought another Victrola which was the low type, because I guess he didn't want me to kill myself trying to play these records.
